title: API 510 Training in Salt Lake City: Vessel Inspector Exam Prep
description: Self-paced API 510 exam prep for Salt Lake City vessel inspectors: five refineries, Utah owner/user rules, cokers and cat crackers. Instructor Q&A.
h1: API 510 Training in Salt Lake City: Pressure Vessel Inspector Exam Prep for Refinery, Contractor and Owner/User Inspectors
html:
API 510 exam prep for vessel inspectors in the Salt Lake valley

Refining in Utah happens in one place. Every operating refinery in the state sits on the northern edge of the Salt Lake valley, in Salt Lake City, North Salt Lake and Woods Cross, close enough that a contract inspector can work at two of them in the same week. Each plant runs crude towers, drums, exchangers, reactors and columns that need an API 510 inspector, and the owners, their inspection contractors and the insurers that write boiler and pressure vessel cover in Utah all employ people who hold, or are working towards, the certification.

This page is for those people. It names the refineries and the vessel-heavy units they run, explains how Utah's boiler and pressure vessel rules decide who may inspect a vessel and how often, lists the damage mechanisms that matter in local service, and works one interval calculation through against both API 510 and the state's own inspection cycle. There is no Atlantis classroom in Salt Lake City: the course is online, self-paced and supported by an instructor who answers your questions, so you can prepare from home, from a contractor's trailer or from a hotel room during a turnaround elsewhere.

Five refineries a short drive apart

The US Energy Information Administration's refinery capacity survey, which reports capacity as of the start of 2026, lists five operable refineries in Utah, all operating, with a combined atmospheric crude distillation capacity of 213,089 barrels per calendar day. The table below gives each one as EIA lists it, with the downstream units in the same survey that add the most pressure vessels to an inspection programme.

A few facts from the owners help a candidate picture the work. Marathon says its plant began operating in 1908, is the largest refinery in Utah, employs about 300 people and processes crude from Utah, Colorado, Wyoming and Canada. Chevron's history page says Standard Oil Company of California built the Salt Lake refinery in 1948 to run 14,000 barrels a day of Rangely crude from north-west Colorado. HF Sinclair places its Woods Cross refinery in West Bountiful and describes it as a high-conversion plant with access to regional sweet and waxy crudes and, by pipeline, to Canadian crude. FJ Management describes the North Salt Lake plant as a complex high-conversion refinery run by its wholly owned subsidiary Big West Oil, with about 250 employees. Silver Eagle's Woods Cross plant is the smallest of the five and, on EIA's figures, has crude and vacuum distillation but no cracking unit.

Who may inspect a pressure vessel under Utah's rules

Utah regulates boilers and pressure vessels through the Labor Commission, under Rule R616-2 of the Utah Administrative Code, administered by the commission's boiler and elevator safety division. Three groups of inspectors appear in the rule, and a Salt Lake candidate will meet all three.

  • State inspectors. The rule makes inspection of vessels within the division's jurisdiction the division's responsibility, carried out by inspectors who have met recognised competency standards and hold the commission's certificate of competency.
  • Deputy inspectors from insurers. An insurance company writing boiler and pressure vessel insurance in Utah can have its inspectors deputised. R616-2-15 requires a deputy to hold a current certification from the National Board of Boiler and Pressure Vessel Inspectors at all times, and keeps the deputy an employee of the sponsoring company, not of the division.
  • Owner/user agents. A business operating pressure vessels in Utah can hold an owner/user certificate from the commission that authorises self-inspection of its unfired pressure vessels. Its owner/user agents are employees who have received the commission's certificate of competency, and they inspect under procedures and frequencies the division establishes.

The rule also sets the state's own inspection cycle. Heat exchangers on high-pressure steam or high-temperature water, and autoclaves above 15 psi steam, are inspected every 24 months; every other vessel under the division's jurisdiction is inspected every 48 months. A vessel that passes receives a Certificate of Inspection and Permit to Operate, and before an internal inspection the owner must at least meet the federal confined space and lockout rules at 29 CFR 1910.146 and 1910.147.

Utah adopts API 510 by edition

Rule R616-2-3 incorporates the 2023 edition of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code for Sections I, IV and VIII, the 2023 National Board Inspection Code, and API 510, Tenth Edition, 2014, with its Section 8 and Appendix A excepted. That is a state rule, not an exam syllabus. API examines each window on the editions named in that window's Publications Effectivity Sheet, so study those, and treat the edition in the Utah rule as a fact about the jurisdiction you work in.

Vessels in Salt Lake service and the damage they collect

The unit list in the table points to the damage mechanisms a local API 510 inspector deals with. API RP 571 describes each of them, and the Body of Knowledge for your window lists which RP 571 sections are examined.

  • Catalytic crackers. Four of the five refineries run one. Reactor and regenerator vessels and their cyclones see catalyst erosion, high temperatures and refractory that can hide shell damage, so inspection planning leans on hot spot surveys and internal access at turnarounds.
  • Coke drums. Chevron's delayed coker is the only one EIA lists in Utah. Coke drums are heated and quenched on every cycle, and thermal fatigue of the shell and skirt is the classic concern on them.
  • Reformers and hydrotreaters. Catalytic reforming appears at four plants, and making low-sulfur fuel needs hydrotreating. Hot hydrogen service brings high temperature hydrogen attack into the vessel programme, while hydrotreater effluent trains can see wet hydrogen sulfide damage and ammonium bisulfide corrosion.
  • Amine and sour water units. Regenerators, contactors and stripper vessels are where amine stress corrosion cracking and wet hydrogen sulfide damage are most often found.

Waxy crude from the Uinta Basin is part of the local picture too. Market analysts describe the basin's black wax and yellow wax crudes as low in sulfur, acid and metals, and Utah's Department of Environmental Quality notes that local refineries can crack the wax in their fluid catalytic cracking units. A low-sulfur crude does not take wet hydrogen sulfide damage off the list, because Canadian and Rocky Mountain crudes also arrive by pipeline and the downstream units generate their own sour streams. What changes with the crude slate is the corrosion rate, and API 510 expects an inspector to notice when a rate stops matching the process.

Cold-weather questions on the Wasatch Front

Salt Lake winters bring a set of vessel questions that the exam also tests. The first is brittle fracture during pressure testing. Section VIII, in UG-99, recommends keeping the metal temperature during a hydrostatic test at least 30°F above the vessel's minimum design metal temperature, without needing to exceed 120°F, and a winter repair test with cold water from a site hydrant can fall short of that unless the inspector plans for it. The second is the nameplate minimum design metal temperature itself, and whether a vessel bought or moved for a new duty is fit for the coldest metal temperature it will see. The third is the impact test and exemption rules in Section VIII that decide whether a material needs impact testing at all. All three sit in the closed-book half of the exam as well as the open-book half, so learn the principle as well as where the clause is.

Worked example: a crude feed surge drum with two clocks

This example uses illustrative figures. A carbon steel crude feed surge drum has an inside diameter of 72 inches, so an inside radius of 36 inches, and a design pressure of 150 psig. Assume an allowable stress of 20,000 psi and a joint efficiency of 0.85 for spot-radiographed seams. The shell's required thickness from the circumferential stress formula in UG-27 is P times R divided by (S times E minus 0.6 times P): 150 × 36 ÷ (17,000 − 90) = 5,400 ÷ 16,910 = 0.319 inch.

The drum entered service with a measured shell thickness of 0.500 inch in 2004. An inspection in 2019 found 0.441 inch at the thinnest location, and the 2025 inspection found 0.414 inch at the same location.

  1. Long-term corrosion rate: (0.500 − 0.414) ÷ 21 years = 0.0041 inch per year.
  2. Short-term corrosion rate: (0.441 − 0.414) ÷ 6 years = 0.0045 inch per year.
  3. API 510 asks the inspector to compare the two and select the rate that best reflects the current process, consulting a corrosion specialist where needed. With the feed unchanged, the faster short-term rate is the prudent choice here.
  4. Remaining life: (0.414 − 0.319) ÷ 0.0045 = 21.1 years.
  5. Internal or on-stream inspection interval: the lesser of half the remaining life, 10.6 years, and 10 years, so 10 years. The external visual inspection interval is the lesser of five years and that internal interval, so five years.

Now the second clock. In Utah this drum, if it is within the division's jurisdiction, also sits on the state's 48-month cycle unless the owner is an owner/user agency working to frequencies the division has set. The inspection plan therefore carries both sets of dates and follows whichever falls first. At the projected rate the shell would be about 0.396 inch at the next state inspection, comfortably above the required thickness, so the state visit is a check on a healthy drum rather than a sign that the code interval was too long. On the exam you will only be asked for the API 510 answer; at work you need both.

Routes into API 510 from Salt Lake City jobs

API counts inspection experience from the last ten years gained while employed by or under contract with an authorized inspection agency, and API 510's definition of that term takes in an owner or user's own inspection organisation and contractors working under its direction, as well as the jurisdiction and qualifying insurers. The amount you need depends on education, and the API 510 certification requirements page sets out every route. Locally, the common ones look like this.

  • Engineers. A bachelor's degree in engineering or technology, for example from the University of Utah or Utah State University, needs one year of supervising or performing pressure vessel inspection. Process and reliability engineers who take on inspection duties can reach that sooner than they expect.
  • Technicians with a two-year qualification. A two-year degree or certificate in engineering or technology needs two years in design, construction, repair, operation or inspection of pressure vessels, one of them in supervision or performance of inspection.
  • Welders and fitters. Salt Lake Community College's Welding Technology programme at its Westpointe campus includes a required course in welding inspection and welding metallurgy, and Davis Technical College in Kaysville runs a welding programme and is an AWS Accredited Test Facility. Welders from either route who move into repair and inspection work usually come in on the high school route, which needs three years including one in inspection.
  • NDT technicians. UT thickness and shear wave technicians on refinery contracts build vessel experience every day, provided their role includes performing inspection activities as API 510 describes them. Atlantis's NDT training for Salt Lake City covers the ASNT SNT-TC-1A methods that lead into that work.

Studying around refinery shifts and turnarounds

Most candidates here are already working, many on rotating shifts or long contract stretches, and the course is built for that. Lessons and practice questions wait where you left them. The Body of Knowledge and effectivity sheet for your window set the reading, and the most useful habit for a shift worker is to tie each study session to one document: a session on UG-27 and the head formulas, another on the API 510 interval rules, another on welding procedure questions from Section IX. Keep the timed practice papers for days off, when you can sit the closed-book and open-book parts back to back the way the real exam runs them. If a calculation will not come out on a night shift, send the question and pick up the instructor's answer when you are back on days.

A turnaround at your own plant is study material in its own right. Internal inspections of drums and columns, repair procedures and pressure tests are where the code clauses stop being abstract, so note what you see and look up the clause that governs it afterwards.

Preparation choices for a Salt Lake candidate

A candidate in Salt Lake City has a few realistic ways to prepare, and each suits a different person.

  • An in-person seminar in another city. Some providers run classroom exam-prep courses on fixed dates elsewhere in the country. That suits someone who studies best in a room and whose employer will cover the travel and the time away.
  • A self-paced online course. Atlantis's course and others like it let you start straight away and keep working through turnarounds and shift changes. It suits people who cannot leave the plant for a week.
  • Employer mentoring. Some inspection groups pair candidates with certified inspectors and review practice questions together. That gives site context no course can, and works best alongside structured exam preparation.
  • Self-study from the codes. Possible for someone disciplined who already knows the documents, though without worked calculations and timed papers it is easy to underestimate the open-book half.

Sponsoring vessel inspectors from a Salt Lake employer

Refiners, inspection contractors and insurers in the valley can enrol one candidate or several, and fees are quoted on request. Each person still applies to API individually and has their own experience verified, so a sponsoring employer helps most by confirming dates and duties on the application promptly. An owner/user agency adding API 510 holders to its inspection group, or a contractor bidding vessel work at more than one Salt Lake refinery, can line candidates up on the same exam window and compare progress through the practice papers. Welding inspectors in the same group may also want the AWS CWI exam prep for Salt Lake City.

faq.q: Is there anywhere in Salt Lake City to take an API 510 preparation class in person?
faq.a: Atlantis does not run one. Its API 510 course is online and self-paced, with an instructor who answers questions as you work, so you can prepare from anywhere in the valley around your shifts. The examination itself is the only part that must be taken in person, at a Prometric test centre. Prometric lists test centres in and around Salt Lake City, and you choose one when you schedule after API approves your application.

faq.q: Does Utah require an owner/user agent to hold API 510 certification?
faq.a: The definitions in Rule R616-2 describe an owner/user agent as an employee of an owner/user agency who is authorised to inspect unfired pressure vessels after receiving the commission's certificate of competency. Those definitions do not themselves name API 510 certification, so ask the Labor Commission's boiler division what it accepts as evidence of competency. Because the same rule adopts API 510 as an inspection code, API 510 certification is the natural credential for that role.

faq.q: Utah's rule adopts the 2014 tenth edition of API 510. Is that the edition I will be examined on?
faq.a: Not necessarily. API sets the editions for each exam window in that window's Publications Effectivity Sheet, and those are the documents you study and the PDFs you will see in the open-book half. The edition named in Rule R616-2-3 tells you what the state has adopted for vessels in Utah. Keep the two separate in your head: one is your syllabus, the other is your jurisdiction.

faq.q: I am an insurer's deputy inspector in Utah with National Board certification. Is API 510 worth adding?
faq.a: It often is, because refinery owners and their contractors work to API 510 for in-service vessels and the certification shows you know that code as well as the National Board Inspection Code. Whether your deputy work counts as qualifying experience depends on what you actually did, and API verifies it from your application. Your National Board certification remains the requirement for your deputy role under R616-2-15.

faq.q: Does inspecting coke drums or catalytic cracker vessels count as API 510 experience?
faq.a: Coke drums, regenerators and reactors are pressure vessels, so supervising or performing their inspection is the kind of work API 510 describes. What API looks at is your role and the dates, verified through your application, rather than the unit. If your work on those vessels was mainly mechanical repair or operation, it can still count on the longer routes for candidates without a degree.

faq.q: I trained as a welder at Salt Lake Community College. How do I get to API 510?
faq.a: Check whether your programme counts as a two-year certificate in engineering or technology. If it does, you need two years in vessel design, construction, repair, operation or inspection, including one year supervising or performing inspection. Otherwise the high school route needs three years with the same one year of inspection. Repair welding on vessels counts toward the broader experience, and a move into an inspection or QC role builds the inspection year.

faq.q: How long is the API 510 exam day, and what should I expect at the test centre?
faq.a: Plan for a 7.5-hour day. After a short tutorial there are 2.75 hours of closed-book questions, a 45-minute break and 3.75 hours of open-book questions, 170 questions in all, of which 140 are scored. You bring no books or notes; for the open-book part the code PDFs are provided on the computer. Practise finding answers in PDFs before you go.

faq.q: Can our refinery enrol its whole inspection group?
faq.a: Yes. A refinery, contractor or insurer in the Salt Lake area can enrol several candidates together, and fees are quoted on request. Each candidate keeps their own progress on the portal and asks the instructor their own questions, so people on different shifts can still prepare for the same exam window. Each person must apply to API separately and meet the eligibility rules individually.
